query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The creep resistance of FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coatings under continuous loading is enhanced by the dual‐phase microstructure, where coherent interfaces between the ductile FCC dendrites and the stronger BCC precipitates serve as effective barriers to dislocation glide and promote load partitioning (including activation of deformation twinning in the FCC phase) that collectively suppress strain localization.
generation.material_initial_state: A protective coating with a dual-phase microstructure comprising oriented FCC dendrites with embedded BCC precipitates and coherent, well‐developed phase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal or mechanical processing route to modify the phase boundary morphology—producing one set of coatings with refined, coherent FCC/BCC interfaces versus a controlled comparison sample processed to yield a more homogeneous (or less well‐defined dual‐phase) microstructure.
generation.conditions: Continuous load (constant stress) creep testing at elevated temperatures (e.g. 500–600°C) simulating service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent FCC/BCC phase boundaries that enable effective load partitioning and retard dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Under sustained stress at elevated temperatures, the phase boundaries impede dislocation glide and delay plastic strain accumulation by encouraging deformation twinning in the FCC phase and by constraining dislocation motion in the BCC regions; this dynamic strain accommodation reduces localized creep deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline with fewer or less coherent phase boundaries, the dual‐phase coating will exhibit a lower creep strain rate, higher apparent stress exponents (indicative of rate‐limiting dislocation processes), and reduced strain localization as evidenced by microstructural analyses (e.g. via TEM/EBSD).
generation.baseline: An alloy coating of similar composition processed to have a single-phase (or less distinctly separated dual-phase) microstructure with poorly defined FCC/BCC interfaces.
generation.boundary: Results are expected under sustained high-temperature mechanical loading typical of creep conditions; differences may diminish outside these elevated temperature and long-duration regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative balance between dislocation pinning at phase boundaries and the role of deformation twinning in strain accommodation remains to be fully clarified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of protective coatings with identical overall chemistry: one set engineered to develop a refined dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure with coherent phase boundaries (via optimized thermal spray and post-treatment processes) and a second set processed to favor a single-phase or poorly defined dual-phase structure. Subject both sets to identical isothermal creep tests at 500–600°C under constant load while monitoring deformation using digital image correlation and microstructural evolution with TEM/EBSD.
measurements: Creep strain rate and total creep strain over time
Dislocation density and distribution via TEM
Phase boundary coherence and evidence of deformation twinning via EBSD/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase coating does not display a statistically significant lower creep strain rate and higher stress exponent along with evidence of strain delocalization (e.g., reduced local strain concentration) compared to the single-phase (or non-optimized dual-phase) coating, then the hypothesis that coherent FCC/BCC interfaces enhance creep resistance is falsified.

AlxCr0.2NbTiV (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8) refractory high-entropy alloys were fabricated by arc melting. The effects of Al content on the microstructure of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were studied using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction. The microhardness, compression properties, and nanoindentation creep properties of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were also tested. The results show that the AlxCr0.2NbTiV series exhibits a BCC single-phase structure. As the Al content increases, the lattice constant of the alloys gradually decreases, and the intensity of the (110) crystal plane diffraction peak increases. cited_evidence.text: The material studied here is a FeCoCrNiAl0.5 alloy, characterized by a two-phase microstructure consisting of 〈001〉-oriented fcc dendrites with fine bcc/B2 precipitates embedded and bounded by a bcc/B2 interdendritic. The intimate two-phase fcc + bcc/B2 microstructure is expected to entail complex heterogeneous strain partitioning between these phases because of their mechanical contrast. Also, heterogeneous grain and phase distributions in addition to segregations (chemical gradients) resulting from the dendritic solidification during casting add to the intricacy of its stress-strain response. Our experiments reveal that this composition shows exceptional work hardening both at 293K and 77K, considerably higher than previously reported hardening rates for e.g. Fe-Mn and Hadfield steels,. Based on the experimental observations elaborated below we attribute the substantial hardening to the combined action of these 3 contributions: (i) the fcc – bcc/B2 interphase boundaries resulting from the dendritic-interdendritic microstructure, (ii) extensive deformation twinning in fcc, (iii) fine and dense bcc/B2 precipitates inside the fcc dendrites.

In this section we present the key experimental observations documenting the stress-strain response of dual-phase FeCoCrNiAl0.5 in relation to its pristine vs. deformed microstructure. After characterizing the undeformed microstructure by EBSD and TEM, the influence of temperature (293K vs. 77K) on the strain-hardening rate is studied and the strain partitioning between fcc and bcc/B2 determined from DIC strain maps. EBSD and (high-resolution) TEM of deformed FeCoCrNiAl0.5 reveal deformation twinning in the fcc phase.

Molecular dynamics is applied to explore the deformation mechanism and crystal structure development of the AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys under nanoimprinting. The influences of crystal structure, alloy composition, grain size, and twin boundary distance on the mechanical properties are carefully analyzed. The imprinting load indicates that the highest loading force is in ascending order with polycrystalline, nano-twinned (NT) polycrystalline, and monocrystalline. The change in alloy composition suggests that the imprinting force increases as the Al content in the alloy increases. The reverse Hall–Petch relation found for the polycrystalline structure, while the Hall–Petch and reverse Hall–Petch relations are discovered in the NT-polycrystalline, which is due to the interactions between the dislocations and grain/twin boundaries (GBs/TBs). The deformation behavior shows that shear strain and local stress are concentrated not only around the punch but also on GBs and adjacent to GBs. The slide and twist of the GBs play a major in controlling the deformation mechanism of polycrystalline structure.
